results.q: How did the workers end up opening the wrong flange at PEMEX?
results.text:
They ended up opening the wrong flange because PEMEX did not have a clear, standardized way to identify the correct equipment for flange opening work. The workers were given a written list and a process sketch, but those were not enough to direct them to the right place. [pemex-045][pemex-025]

The report says the Repcon boilermakers relied on flange-locking devices and blind tags they were familiar with from turnaround work. In this case, the tag for the intended blind was out of sight, and a different flange-locking device on a visually similar line led them to believe they had found the right location. [pemex-045][pemex-001]

A key problem was that the work permit and job setup did not force a clear, shared check of the exact opening point by both the operator and the workers. The permit also lacked a defined hold point, so the operators, foreman, and boilermakers understood the steps differently. As a result, the workers chose an active hydrogen sulfide line instead of the intended empty one. [pemex-046]

The report also says the workers thought they were still in a shutdown turnaround unit, not a partially operating unit, so they were looking for the kinds of indicators used in turnaround work rather than a positive identification of the live equipment. [pemex-046][pemex-001]

results.q: How did the workers end up opening the wrong flange at PEMEX?
results.text:
They ended up opening the wrong flange because the location of the blind was not clearly marked, and the workers fell back on visual cues that were not meant to identify opening points. The boiler makers said they looked for orange-and-blue blind tags or unlocked red flange-locking devices instead of using the blind list or drawing, because the list and drawing did not clearly show where each flange was located [pemex-012][pemex-018]. PEMEX Deer Park did not have a standardized process for flange opening and blind removal, so the workers used flange-locking devices as a cue even though those devices were intended to secure installed blinds, not identify equipment for opening [pemex-025][pemex-019].

For Blind 407, the workers saw an unlocked flange-locking device on the ARU7 piping and believed that was the intended work location [pemex-012][pemex-019]. In reality, Blind 407 was on a different piping segment about 5 feet away [pemex-012]. The CSB also said the permit was too broad: it covered blinds with different hazards, so the operator was not present when the acid gas blind was opened, which removed another safeguard that could have caught the mistake [pemex-033][pemex-046].

results.q: What caused the furnace explosion at Shell Polymers Monaca?
results.text:
The CSB said the furnace exploded because both motor-operated isolation valves were opened at the same time by mistake. That created a path for cracked gas to flow back into Furnace 5’s firebox, where the lit pilots ignited it. [monaca-037][monaca-015][monaca-016]

Several things contributed. Shell assigned a PACO engineer who had never done that task before. Shell also relied on administrative controls instead of an engineered way to prevent backflow. And the valve-control screen was confusing: it put three similar valves on one diagram without clear labels, which increased the chance of human error. [monaca-037][monaca-012][monaca-001]

In the sequence the report describes, the furnace was being returned to operation after coke-trap cleaning. Once the furnace-side valve was open and the tower-side valve started opening, an unintended flow path let cracked gas backflow into the lower-pressure firebox. The gas accumulated, then ignited about 6 minutes after the bad valve command. [monaca-015][monaca-016][monaca-012]

results.q: What caused the furnace explosion at Shell Polymers Monaca?
results.text:
Shell Polymers Monaca said the explosion was caused by the inadvertent simultaneous opening of both motor-operated valves used to isolate Furnace 5. That opened a path for cracked gas to backflow into the furnace firebox, where lit pilots ignited it and caused the explosion. [monaca-037]

Several things contributed. Shell had relied on administrative controls instead of an engineered control to prevent backflow. The engineer who manipulated the valves had limited process knowledge and had not done that task before. The safety system’s human-machine interface also made the valves hard to distinguish because it put all three on one diagram without clear labels. [monaca-037][monaca-002]

In the sequence leading up to the explosion, the unintended flow path let cracked gas from a higher-pressure header backflow into the Furnace 5 firebox. The gas accumulated there until it contacted the lit pilots and ignited. [monaca-015][monaca-016]

results.q: What did the CSB recommend to Shell Polymers?
results.text:
CSB recommended two actions to Shell Polymers Monaca:

1. Review the ethane cracking unit process hazard analysis to find process deviations that are controlled only by administrative measures, and add an inherently safer design or an engineered control for any scenario that could lead to a fatality, serious injury, or major property damage. [monaca-038]  
2. Based on licensor input and good industry practices, implement and maintain an engineered control to stop cracked gas from flowing backward into a furnace during all modes of furnace operation. [monaca-038]

The CSB also said Shell had already taken some corrective actions after the incident, so it was not making additional recommendations on those specific issues. But it urged Shell to make sure the new controls are fully implemented and consistently followed for all furnaces at the site, and to ensure the furnace coke traps are cleaned periodically according to Linde’s guidance. [monaca-038]

results.q: What mechanical integrity problems did the CSB find in the 2023 Honeywell reboiler explosion?
results.text:
The CSB found several mechanical integrity problems in the 2023 Honeywell Geismar reboiler explosion. Honeywell’s reliability group inspected the reboiler in October 2021 and determined the carbon steel shell was approaching Tmin and needed replacement, but the site did not adequately respond to that deficiency, communicate it to all affected people, or resolve it before failure. [geismar-030][geismar-067]

The site also failed to preserve the problem in its maintenance systems. No SAP deficiency notification was created, no SAP notification was created for the next inspection date, and no DMAPS action item was created. As a result, when the maintenance engineer left in April 2022, the site lost active knowledge of the reboiler’s condition and no follow-up inspection was scheduled or performed. [geismar-034][geismar-035]

More broadly, the CSB said Honeywell Geismar’s MI system was siloed. Key people, departments, and functions did not know the shell’s condition or how urgently it needed replacement, and Honeywell allowed the shell to corrode to failure three times, with the last failure causing a catastrophic BLEVE. [geismar-067]

results.q: What mechanical integrity problems did the CSB find in the 2023 Honeywell reboiler explosion?
results.text:
The CSB found several mechanical integrity problems in the 2023 Honeywell Geismar reboiler explosion. The biggest one was that Honeywell knew the reboiler shell was thinning and nearing Tmin, but did not adequately respond to that deficiency before the shell failed [geismar-030][geismar-031].

After the October 2021 inspection, Honeywell’s own reliability group had enough information to treat the shell as a deficiency. The CSB said the site should have documented it in SAP and DMAPS, created a record for the next inspection, and tracked corrective action to completion. It did none of those things [geismar-034][geismar-031].

The CSB also found the problem was not well communicated. After the inspection, the deficiency was likely only informally told to one maintenance engineer. Other important people at the site did not have visibility to it, and Honeywell’s MI functions were siloed [geismar-031][geismar-034].

The report also says Honeywell never performed a documented fitness-for-service evaluation, even though the inspection form said the shell was “fit for service” and also recommended replacing the shell. The CSB found no support for the “fit for service” statement [geismar-028].

After the failure, metallurgical examination found the shell had severely thinned from HF corrosion, with some locations as thin as 0.030 inches, about 95 percent thickness loss [geismar-028].

results.q: Why was Reactor 6's relief system inadequate at Givaudan?
results.text:
Reactor 6’s relief system was inadequate because it was too small for the runaway sugar decomposition reaction that happened that day. The CSB said the system did function as designed, but it could not relieve the gas and pressure fast enough, so pressure kept rising until Reactor 6 ruptured. [givaudan-035][givaudan-033]

The report says the relief system on Reactor 6 was a 4-inch rupture disc in series with a 4-inch pressure relief valve. It was based on the design of Reactor 2, but the facility had no documentation showing the design basis for that earlier system. [givaudan-033]

The CSB’s modeling found that Reactor 6 would have needed a relief area of at least 16.74 square inches to meet code compliance for the incident scenario. It says that would have meant a much larger 6R10 relief valve, or else removing the pressure relief valve and using only the 4-inch rupture disc. [givaudan-035]

So the problem was not a mechanical failure. It was that the installed relief capacity was not enough for the accelerated decomposition reaction once the vent valve had failed closed and the reactor kept generating heat and gas. [givaudan-034][givaudan-035]

results.q: Why was Reactor 6's relief system inadequate at Givaudan?
results.text:
Reactor 6’s relief system was inadequate because it was too small for the runaway sugar decomposition reaction that happened that day. The CSB said the system itself worked as designed, but it was undersized, so it could not relieve the gases and pressure fast enough and Reactor 6 kept pressurizing until it ruptured. [givaudan-035][givaudan-061]

The report says the facility based Reactor 6’s relief system on Reactor 2’s design, but it did not have documentation showing that design basis. It also did not use the earlier 2012 reactivity testing when it designed Reactors 5 and 6, even though that testing had led to larger relief systems for Reactors 3 and 4. Because of that, Reactor 6 ended up with the same 4.186-square-inch relief valve size used on Reactor 2, rather than a larger system sized for the sugar decomposition hazard. [givaudan-033][givaudan-016][givaudan-063]

The CSB’s modeling found that the existing pressure relief system would have needed to be four times larger to prevent the rupture, or a 4-inch rupture disc alone could have provided enough relief capacity. [givaudan-035][givaudan-061]

results.q: What was the means-of-egress problem in the Wacker incident?
results.text:
The means-of-egress problem was that the fifth-floor platform had only one staircase, and when the hydrogen chloride cloud formed, workers could not safely reach it because it was on the same side they would have had to pass through. [wacker-013][wacker-001]

Wacker had already flagged this as a hazard in its process hazard analysis three months earlier. The analysis specifically asked what would happen if there were an HCl leak while people were on the 4th or 5th floor and recommended a ladder or other alternate exit on the opposite end of the structure, but that second exit was not installed before the incident. [wacker-027]

The CSB said this limited egress contributed to the severity of the event. [wacker-034]

results.q: What was the means-of-egress problem in the Wacker incident?
results.text:
The means-of-egress problem was that the fifth-floor platform had only one staircase out. When the hydrogen chloride cloud formed, that single exit was effectively blocked because workers could not see their surroundings or safely reach the stairs through the cloud. [wacker-001][wacker-013]

Wacker had identified this risk before the incident. In a Process Hazard Analysis three months earlier, employees noted the need for a second exit route on the structure, but Wacker did not install one before the release. [wacker-027][wacker-033]

The CSB said this limited egress made the event worse. Had there been a safer second exit, the workers trapped on the fifth floor may have been able to get out without climbing down the piping, which led to the fatal fall and serious injuries. [wacker-027][wacker-034]

results.q: Which incidents involved problems with pressure relief systems?
results.text:
The incidents that involved pressure relief system problems were **Dow Louisiana Operations** and **Givaudan Sense Colour**. [dow-030][dow-026][dow-025][givaudan-033][givaudan-035]

At **Dow Louisiana**, the issue was the emergency pressure relief system on the product cooler and connected piping. The reports say the rupture disc and pressure relief valve were part of that system, the relief piping was routed to the reflux drum, and the system did not keep an inert atmosphere in the piping between the rupture disc and the PRV. The CSB said Dow’s pressure relief design and its later loss of nitrogen inerting contributed to the incident. [dow-006][dow-030][dow-026]

At **Givaudan Sense Colour**, the Reactor 6 emergency pressure relief system was too small for the runaway reaction that occurred. The reports say the system had a rupture disc and pressure relief valve in series, it functioned mechanically, but it could not relieve enough pressure and gas to prevent Reactor 6 from rupturing. [givaudan-033][givaudan-034][givaudan-035]

The other four reports do not describe a pressure relief system problem as a central issue.

results.q: Which incidents involved problems with pressure relief systems?
results.text:
Based on the six reports, the incidents with pressure relief system problems were:

- **Dow Louisiana Operations**: the report says the ethylene oxide pressure relief piping between the rupture disc and PRV lost its inert nitrogen atmosphere, and that Dow lacked effective monitoring and design controls for that pressure relief system. The report also says Dow’s decision to vent the product cooler’s pressure relief to the reflux drum increased the severity of the incident. [dow-026][dow-028][dow-030]

- **Givaudan Sense Colour**: the report says Reactor 6 had an emergency pressure relief system, but it was **undersized** for the runaway decomposition reaction, so it could not adequately relieve the gas and pressure and the reactor ruptured. [givaudan-033][givaudan-035]

The other reports you asked me to check did **not** identify pressure relief system problems as the issue:
- **PEMEX Deer Park** was about wrong equipment identification and opening active piping. [pemex-017][pemex-045]
- **Shell Polymers Monaca** was about the motor-operated valve control logic and administrative controls. [monaca-002][monaca-014]
- **Honeywell Geismar** was about corrosion, reboiler failure, and safe work practices. [geismar-024][geismar-034][geismar-055]
- **Wacker Polysilicon** was about over-torquing a flange on live HCl piping. [wacker-001][wacker-034]

So, from these six reports, the ones involving pressure relief system problems were **Dow Louisiana Operations** and **Givaudan Sense Colour**.

results.q: What do the PEMEX and Wacker incidents have in common?
results.text:
PEMEX and Wacker have several things in common. In both incidents, contractor workers were doing maintenance work on live process equipment and opened or stressed the wrong equipment or the wrong connection, which released a toxic gas. In PEMEX, workers opened the wrong piping and released hydrogen sulfide; in Wacker, excessive torque on flange bolts cracked piping and released hydrogen chloride. [pemex-013][wacker-034]

In both cases, the companies lacked clear job-specific controls for the work. PEMEX did not have an effective standardized system to identify the exact equipment to be opened, and its permit did not control the hazards of opening piping in an operating unit. [pemex-017][pemex-046] Wacker did not have written procedures for the torquing task and did not treat the work as requiring hazardous-energy control. [wacker-001][wacker-033]

Both incidents also exposed workers who were not part of the task itself. At PEMEX, the hydrogen sulfide spread to nearby contractors and killed another worker downwind. [pemex-001][pemex-015] At Wacker, a separate contractor crew was working nearby and was unnecessarily exposed to the HCl release. [wacker-002][wacker-033]

A final common point is that both reports say better planning and clearer work controls could have prevented or reduced the harm. [pemex-046][wacker-034]

results.q: What do the PEMEX and Wacker incidents have in common?
results.text:
The PEMEX and Wacker incidents both involved a maintenance task on live process equipment that went wrong and released a toxic gas. In PEMEX, workers opened the wrong piping, which released pressurized hydrogen sulfide [pemex-048][pemex-001]. In Wacker, a contractor over-torqued bolts on an HCl flange connection, which fractured equipment and released gaseous hydrogen chloride [wacker-034][wacker-001].

They also had the same broad safety theme: the companies did not adequately control the hazards of the work before it started. PEMEX did not clearly identify the correct equipment and did not properly control the hazards of opening piping in an operating unit [pemex-048][pemex-002]. Wacker did not have a written procedure for the torquing task and did not treat the work as requiring hazardous energy control or a risk analysis before the safe work permit was issued [wacker-034][wacker-001].

Both incidents harmed contractors. PEMEX killed two contract workers and exposed many others, leading to shelter-in-place orders [pemex-016][pemex-015]. Wacker killed one contractor and seriously injured two others, partly because the release and the platform layout made escape difficult [wacker-001][wacker-034].

So, in plain terms: both were contractor maintenance jobs on hazardous live equipment, and both failed because the work was not clearly identified, not adequately planned, and not well controlled [pemex-048][wacker-034].

results.q: Which of the reports made recommendations to OSHA?
results.text:
The reports that made recommendations to OSHA are:

- **Givaudan Sense Colour** — it reiterated a prior CSB recommendation to OSHA to amend the PSM standard to better cover reactive hazards [givaudan-066][givaudan-059].
- **Honeywell Geismar** — it reiterated a prior CSB recommendation to OSHA to require management of organizational and personnel change in PSM [geismar-072][geismar-043].
- **Wacker Polysilicon** — it made new recommendations to OSHA on SIMOPs, including a standard or changes to existing standards and a safety product on SIMOPs [wacker-035][wacker-036].

The other three reports did **not** make recommendations to OSHA:
- **PEMEX Deer Park** recommended actions to PEMEX Deer Park and ASME, not OSHA [pemex-003][pemex-049].
- **Shell Polymers Monaca** recommended actions to Shell, not OSHA [monaca-003][monaca-038].
- **Dow Louisiana Operations** recommended actions to Dow, NFPA, and ASSP, not OSHA [dow-003][dow-033].

results.q: Has PEMEX closed the CSB's recommendations yet?
results.text:
The reports don’t say that PEMEX has closed those recommendations yet. The PEMEX Deer Park report lists recommendations to PEMEX Deer Park and to ASME, but it does not give a closure or status update for them. [pemex-049][pemex-003]

The report does say PEMEX made some post-incident improvements: it added signs to distinguish turnaround areas from run-and-maintain areas, and it planned a feather flag at the jobsite. It also says that because PEMEX Deer Park made improvements after the incident to ensure equipment is accurately identified when removing blinds, the CSB did not issue a recommendation on positive equipment identification. [pemex-041][pemex-003]

Status after publication is outside what these reports cover.
